name: dev-facts
description: Check the facts a developer asks for again and again: when a software version reaches end of life, whether the runtimes a repository pins are still supported, what an open-source license is, whether a web feature works in a browser, what an RFC says about itself and what changed between two versions of a package.

interface.longDescription:
Check the facts a developer asks for again and again: when a software version reaches end of life, whether the runtimes a repository pins are still supported, what an open-source license is, whether a web feature works in a browser, what an RFC says about itself and what changed between two versions of a package.

Ask "is Node.js 20 still supported?", "is anything in this repo past end of life?", "is the MIT license OSI approved?", "can I use CSS container queries in Safari?", "which RFC obsoletes RFC 2616?" or "what changed in express between 4.18.2 and 5.1.0?".

For a repository, pass the files that pin runtimes (package.json, .nvmrc, .python-version, pyproject.toml, go.mod, a Dockerfile or compose file, .tool-versions, mise.toml, .ruby-version, a Gemfile, composer.json or global.json) and get one row per runtime with its end-of-life date, days left, latest patch and the next supported cycle.

It reads five public sources: endoflife.date for release cycles and support dates, the SPDX License List for license identifiers and OSI and FSF status, webstatus.dev for Baseline status and the first browser version that supports a web feature, the RFC Editor and IETF Datatracker for RFC status, abstracts and obsoleting links, and GitHub releases and changelog files for the notes of each release in a version range.

Every answer names its source and the date of the data. endoflife.date is maintained by volunteers, so confirm a date with the vendor before a contract or compliance decision. A license answer identifies a license and does not say what it lets you do: it is not legal advice.

It does not scan packages for vulnerabilities or health: use the Package Health Check plugin for that.

It stores nothing about you: answers are cached for a few hours and the only lasting record is a daily count of calls per tool.
capabilities: Shows whether a version of a product has reached end of life, with its end-of-life and LTS dates
Lists the release cycles of a product that are still supported, newest first, with the latest patch
Reads the runtime pins in a repo (Node.js, Python, Go, Ruby, PHP, .NET, Docker images) and flags any past end of life
Looks up an SPDX license by identifier or name: OSI approved, FSF free, deprecated or not
Shows the first release of each major browser that supports a web feature, and its Baseline status
Looks up an RFC by number or title words: status, abstract, and the RFCs that obsolete or update it
Lists the GitHub release notes of an npm or PyPI package between 2 versions and flags breaking changes
Names the source and the date of its data in every answer
defaultPrompt: Is Node.js 20 still supported, and when does it reach end of life?
Is the MIT license OSI approved?
Can I use CSS container queries in Safari?

positive.description: status ok with release cycle 20, its end-of-life date and whether that date has passed, the LTS dates, the latest 20.x patch, the cycles still supported, and the endoflife.date source with the as-of date. Check against: https://endoflife.date/api/v1/products/nodejs
positive.prompt: Is Node.js 20 still supported and when does it reach end of life?
positive.expected_behavior: Calls get_eol_status with product "nodejs" and version "20".

positive.description: status ok with the express releases after 4.18.2 up to 4.21.2, newest first, each with its date, link and a short excerpt of its notes, the breaking versions if any, complete true, a GitHub compare link, and the source with the as-of date. Check against: https://github.com/expressjs/express/releases.atom
positive.prompt: What changed in express between 4.18.2 and 4.21.2? Anything breaking?
positive.expected_behavior: Calls get_release_notes with name "express", fromVersion "4.18.2" and toVersion "4.21.2".

positive.description: status ok with id "MIT", the name "MIT License", osiApproved true, fsfLibre true, deprecated false, the SPDX page link and the note that this is not legal advice. Check against: https://spdx.org/licenses/MIT.json
positive.prompt: Is the MIT license OSI approved and what is its SPDX id?

positive.description: status ok with one row per pin, past end of life first: Node.js 18 from the >=18 range and Node.js 20 past end of life, Debian 11 (bullseye) as the image's base, Python 3.11 still supported, each with its end-of-life date, days left, latest patch and next supported cycle, and the endoflife.date source with the as-of date. Check against: https://endoflife.date/api/v1/products/nodejs
positive.prompt: Are the runtimes in my repo still supported? package.json has "engines": {"node": ">=18"}, .nvmrc says 20, and the Dockerfile starts with FROM python:3.11-slim-bullseye.
positive.expected_behavior: Calls check_runtime_eol once with the three files: package.json with the engines field, .nvmrc with "20" and a Dockerfile with the FROM line.

positive.description: status ok with RFC 2616 (HTTP/1.1), its historic status, and an obsoletedBy list that names RFCs 7230 to 7235, with the source and as-of date. Check against: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2616.json

negative.description: Package vulnerabilities and health belong to Package Health Check; this plugin covers versions, end of life, licenses and browser support. Expected: Does not use the Dev Facts tools to answer. Says this plugin does not cover package vulnerabilities.
The plugin looks up dated reference facts; it does not teach programming. Expected: Does not call a tool. Answers from general knowledge or points to the React documentation.

The plugin identifies existing SPDX licenses; it does not write or advise on licenses. Expected: Does not call a tool to draft a license. May use check_license to look up a named license, and says it is not legal advice.
negative.prompt: Write a license for my project.

publication.release_notes: 1.2.0: adds check_runtime_eol, which reads the runtime pins in a repository's files (package.json engines, .nvmrc, .python-version, pyproject.toml, go.mod, Dockerfile and compose images, .tool-versions, mise.toml, .ruby-version, Gemfile, composer.json, global.json) and returns each runtime's end-of-life date, days left, latest patch and next supported cycle from endoflife.date. 1.1.0: adds get_release_notes, the GitHub release notes of an npm or PyPI package (or a GitHub repository) between 2 versions, with breaking changes flagged and the changelog file read when the release list does not reach back far enough. 1.0.0: first release. Reads endoflife.date, the SPDX License List, webstatus.dev and the RFC Editor: end-of-life status, license check, browser support and RFC lookup. Answers are cached for up to a day; read-only, no sign-in.
